subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The Value Function: An S-Curve
description: Learn The Value Function: An S-Curve in one minute.

hook.text: Gaining $100 feels good. But losing $100 hurts about twice as much. The curve isn't symmetrical.

buildup.text: Prospect theory's value function is S-shaped: concave for gains, convex and steeper for losses.

discovery.text: The steeper loss side means losses loom larger than equivalent gains. This asymmetry drives most decisions.

twist.text: The curve also flattens at extremes. Gaining $1 million vs $1.1 million feels tiny. The first million matters most.

climax.text: This simple S-curve explains gambling, insurance buying, risk aversion for gains, and risk seeking for losses.

punchline.text: One curve explains a thousand irrational choices.

quiz.question: What shape is the prospect theory value function?
options: S-shaped, steeper on the loss side

details.summary: Prospect theory's value function is an S-shaped curve that is steeper for losses than gains and concave above the reference point and convex below it, meaning gains have diminishing returns while losses have diminishing sensitivity as they grow larger.
details.whyItMatters: The S-curve mathematically captures loss aversion and diminishing sensitivity in a single elegant function. It replaced the linear utility assumption and became the foundation for predicting real human choice behavior.
takeaways: The curve is steeper for losses, reflecting loss aversion
Gains show diminishing marginal value as they increase
Losses show diminishing marginal pain as they deepen

faq.question: What does the S-shape of the value function mean practically?
faq.answer: Going from $0 to $100 feels great. Going from $100 to $200 feels good but less so. Going from $900 to $1000 barely registers. Similarly, the first $100 loss hurts terribly, but the difference between losing $900 and $1000 feels minor.

faq.question: Why is diminishing sensitivity important for pricing?
faq.answer: A $10 discount on a $20 item feels huge. The same $10 discount on a $500 item feels negligible. Diminishing sensitivity means the impact of a price change depends on the reference price, not the absolute amount saved.
